descs.t: The US Supreme Court has rejected the Trump administration's emergency request to make California set aside roughly 20,000 mail ballots from voters the federal government flagged as likely noncitizens. A federal judge, James Boasberg, had already blocked the Justice Department's demand. We walk through what was asked, what the courts decided and what it means for Tuesday's count.

The Supreme Court turned down the Trump administration's bid to have California sideline about 20,000 mail ballots the Justice Department says may have come from noncitizens. Critics of the request say the federal data is flawed, while the administration says noncitizen voting dilutes lawful votes. We look at both claims and what the ruling settles before the midterms.

The Trump administration wanted roughly 20,000 California mail ballots set aside as likely noncitizen votes, and the Supreme Court said no. A US attorney says 34 noncitizens in California have now been charged with illegally registering and voting, while Gavin Newsom calls the federal push intimidation. We break down the fight over who gets counted on the eve of the vote.

intro.plain: Big ruling right before Tuesday. The Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration's emergency request to make California set aside about 20,000 mail ballots the federal government flagged as likely noncitizen votes. A federal judge had already blocked the same demand. So those ballots get counted. Chat, do you think the court got this right?
intro.mid: The Supreme Court just said no to the Trump administration on California's ballots. Washington wanted roughly 20,000 mail ballots from suspected noncitizens set aside; the court refused, after Judge Boasberg also blocked the Justice Department. Critics say the federal list is flawed, the administration says noncitizen votes dilute lawful ones. Chat, which side has the stronger case?
intro.bold: Twenty thousand flagged ballots, and the Supreme Court says California counts them all. The Trump administration called them likely noncitizen votes, a US attorney says 34 noncitizens in the state have already been charged, and Gavin Newsom calls the push intimidation. This is a fight over who gets to decide an election. Chat, where do you stand?

hook.plain: The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to set aside roughly 20,000 California mail ballots. The court refused. Here is what was asked, why it failed and what happens to those ballots.
hook.mid: Two courts, one answer: California keeps counting about 20,000 ballots the federal government flagged as likely noncitizen votes. Here is the case each side made and what the ruling settles.
hook.bold: Thirty four noncitizens charged, 20,000 ballots flagged, and the Supreme Court still says count them. Here is the ballot fight in California the night before the country votes.

descs.t: Texas early voting closed with 7,705,786 votes, about 74.1% of projected final turnout, ahead of Tuesday's Senate race between Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico. Recent polls range from Paxton ahead by 0.6 to Talarico ahead by 4. We go through the numbers and what they can and cannot tell us.

With 7.7 million early votes in, Texas heads into Tuesday with a Senate race the polls cannot agree on: Trafalgar has Ken Paxton up 0.6, YouGov has James Talarico up 4. The governor's race between Greg Abbott and Gina Hinojosa also looks close in some polls. We look at where Texas really stands.

Texas turned out in near presidential numbers before Election Day, and Ken Paxton's Senate race against James Talarico is within a point in one final poll. Democrats talk about flipping the state, Republicans say Latino men are sticking with Trump. We break down the early vote and what it means for Tuesday.

intro.plain: Texas early voting is done: 7,705,786 votes, about 74.1% of the projected turnout. The Senate race is Ken Paxton against James Talarico, and the final polls disagree, from Paxton up 0.6 to Talarico up 4. Chat, if you are in Texas, did you vote early, and how does it feel on the ground?
intro.mid: Texas just finished early voting with 7.7 million ballots. One final poll has Ken Paxton ahead by 0.6, another has James Talarico ahead by 4. The governor's race may be close too. That is not the Texas we are used to. Chat, is this the year Texas surprises everyone, or is it hype?
intro.bold: Texas turned out in force: 7.7 million early votes, and Ken Paxton's Senate race is within a point in one final poll. Democrats think they can flip it, Republicans say the base is holding. Two days out, Texas is a real fight. So chat, call it now: Paxton or Talarico?

hook.plain: Texas early voting closed with 7,705,786 votes. Here is what the numbers and the final polls say about the Senate race.
hook.mid: One poll says Paxton by 0.6. Another says Talarico by 4. Here is what 7.7 million early votes tell us about Texas.
hook.bold: Texas is voting like a swing state. Here is the early vote, the polls, and why Ken Paxton's seat is suddenly a fight.

descs.t: A federal judge in Alaska has dismissed the Justice Department's lawsuit over the state's Senate race, where a second Dan Sullivan appears on the ballot beside Republican Senator Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola. The DOJ says it will appeal. We walk through what the suit asked for, why it was thrown out, and what happens next.

Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed the DOJ's Decoy Dan lawsuit in Alaska, and the department says it is appealing. President Trump says Chuck Schumer and Marc Elias should be held responsible for the second Dan Sullivan on the ballot, while one poll shows Peltola and Sullivan tied at 50 percent. We look at how a duplicate name could matter under ranked choice.

Two men named Dan Sullivan are on Alaska's Senate ballot, a court just tossed the DOJ's attempt to step in, and Trump calls it election fraud at the highest level. With the race tied in one poll, every confused ballot could count. We break down the fight, the appeal, and whether voters can trust the result.

intro.plain: A federal judge in Alaska has thrown out the Justice Department's lawsuit over the Senate race, where a second Dan Sullivan is on the ballot next to the real Senator Dan Sullivan and Mary Peltola. The DOJ says it will appeal. So what was the suit about, and does it change anything before the vote? Chat, have you ever seen two candidates with the same name on one ballot?
intro.mid: Alaska's Senate race has two Dan Sullivans on the ballot, and a judge just dismissed the DOJ's lawsuit over it. The DOJ is appealing, Trump is blaming Schumer and Marc Elias, and one poll has Peltola and Sullivan tied at 50 percent. In a race that close, a name could matter. Chat, tell me: is this a dirty trick or a nothing story?
intro.bold: Two Dan Sullivans, one Senate seat, and a race tied at 50 percent in one poll. A judge just tossed the DOJ's lawsuit, the DOJ says it will appeal, and Trump calls it election fraud at the highest level. If a duplicate name decides Alaska, who answers for it? Chat, call it: should a decoy name ever be allowed on a ballot?

hook.plain: A judge has dismissed the DOJ's lawsuit over Alaska's Senate ballot, which carries two Dan Sullivans. The DOJ says it will appeal. Here is what the case was about.
hook.mid: Alaska's Senate race is tied in one poll, and there are two Dan Sullivans on the ballot. A judge just threw out the DOJ's challenge. Here is what that means.
hook.bold: Two Dan Sullivans on one ballot, a dead even race, and a lawsuit just tossed out of court. Here is how a single name could decide Alaska's Senate seat.

descs.t: Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens has endorsed Republican Mike Rogers over Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed in the Michigan Senate race. Former Congressman Hansen Clarke and other Michigan Democrats have since urged voters to consider a split ticket. We walk through what Stevens said, how her party reacted and what the latest polls show.

Haley Stevens broke with the Democratic Party to back Mike Rogers for the Michigan Senate seat, saying she did not like seeing the nominee campaign with someone who said the country deserved 9/11. Reports say some House Democrats are privately pushing to expel her from their caucus. We look at what the split means for El-Sayed and for the party.

Haley Stevens put her career on the line to stop Abdul El-Sayed from taking a Michigan Senate seat, and the backlash from her own party was instant. Now other Michigan Democrats are telling voters to split their ticket. We break down the fight, the attacks on Stevens, and whether Michigan follows her.

intro.plain: Michigan votes today, and the Senate race just got a twist. Democratic Congresswoman Haley Stevens endorsed Republican Mike Rogers over her own party's nominee, Abdul El-Sayed. Former Congressman Hansen Clarke followed, and some local Democrats are urging a split ticket. Several polls still show El-Sayed ahead. So tell me in the chat: does an endorsement like this change your vote, or not?
intro.mid: A sitting Democrat just told Michigan to elect a Republican. Haley Stevens says she does not like seeing her party's nominee campaign beside someone who said the country deserved 9/11, and her party turned on her fast, with reports that some House Democrats want her out of the caucus. That fight lands on election day. Chat, is Stevens breaking her party, or is her party breaking itself?
intro.bold: Haley Stevens did what almost no politician does: she broke with her party in public, on the eve of the vote. She backed Mike Rogers over Abdul El-Sayed, and the attacks came within hours, from cable news to her own colleagues. Now other Michigan Democrats are following her. Polls open today. Chat, tell me straight: was this courage, or the end of her career?

hook.plain: A Democratic congresswoman has endorsed the Republican in Michigan's Senate race, and others are following. Here is what Haley Stevens said, how her party answered, and what it could mean at the ballot box.
hook.mid: Haley Stevens says she could not stand behind a nominee campaigning with someone who said the country deserved 9/11. Her party's answer was fury. Here is the fight, and what it tells you about the Democrats right now.
hook.bold: On the eve of the vote, a Democrat told Michigan to elect a Republican, and her own party tore into her. Here is why Haley Stevens says she did it, and why she is not alone.
